name: Apple
summary: Apple's interviews are usually run by the team you would join, and candidates commonly describe them as deep rather than broad: interviewers go several levels into your own projects and your area of expertise. Many report a loop with several team members and the hiring manager, with questions that probe quality, attention to detail and the user's experience.
rounds: One or two phone or video interviews with the team
Onsite or virtual loop with several team members, often including the hiring manager

questions.text: Tell me about a product you love and what you'd change about it.
covers: A specific product and the detail that makes it great for you
One change, the user problem it solves, and what it might cost
How you'd know the change made the experience better

questions.text: Walk me through the work you're proudest of, in detail.
covers: The problem and why it was hard
Your own decisions, at the level of design, code or hardware details
The result, and what you'd improve if you did it again

questions.text: Tell me about a time you pushed back on a decision because quality would suffer.
covers: The decision and the quality risk you saw
How you made your case, with evidence rather than opinion
What was decided and what it meant for users

questions.text: Tell me about a time you worked closely with another discipline, such as design or hardware, to ship something.
covers: What each side needed and where the tension was
How you learned enough of their world to work well together
What shipped and how the collaboration shaped it

questions.text: Tell me about a time you noticed a small detail that others had missed. Why did it matter?
covers: The detail and how you spotted it
Why it mattered to users or to the product's quality
What you did about it and what changed

questions.text: Tell me about a time you had to keep information confidential while still working well with others.
covers: Why the information had to stay private, without revealing it now
How you stayed helpful to colleagues without sharing too much
What you learned about balancing openness and discretion

questions.text: Tell me about something you shipped that had a problem. What did you do?
covers: The problem and how it was found
Your part in it, owned plainly, and the fix
What you now check before shipping

questions.text: How would you make an app feel fast and smooth on a phone? What would you measure?
covers: Launch time, dropped frames while scrolling, and responsiveness to taps
Keeping heavy work off the main thread, and profiling before optimising
Battery and memory use as guardrails

questions.text: How would you protect a user's privacy when designing a feature that uses their location?
covers: Collecting only what the feature needs, as coarsely as possible
Processing on the device where you can, and keeping data briefly
Clear permission prompts and controls the user understands

questions.text: How would you test a camera feature across many lighting conditions, devices and users before release?
covers: A test matrix: lighting, motion, skin tones, device models
Automated tests plus human review for what's hard to measure
Metrics and a release bar, and how you'd use feedback from early testers

questions.text: Explain how memory is managed in a language you use, such as reference counting in Swift, and a bug it can cause.
covers: How the language frees memory: reference counting, garbage collection or manual
A typical bug, such as a retain cycle or a dangling pointer
How you'd find it with tools and fix it, for example with weak references

questions.text: How would you make a feature usable for someone who relies on a screen reader?
covers: Meaningful labels, a sensible reading order and grouping of elements
Testing with the screen reader yourself and with people who use one
Other needs too: text size, contrast, motion

questions.text: Why Apple, and why this team in particular?
covers: What the team works on, in your own words
A link to your expertise or something you've built
What you'd bring and what you want to learn

questions.text: What questions do you have about the team and how it works?
covers: Questions about how the team works with other teams
What great work looks like in the role after a year
Questions that respect confidentiality: ask about ways of working, not unreleased products

tips: Go deep: expect follow-ups several levels into your own projects.
Show you care about the details users notice.
Know your résumé thoroughly: pick two projects and prepare to explain every decision, number and trade-off in them.
Apple's careers site lists shared values such as accessibility, privacy and the environment; if your team's work touches one, be ready to discuss it.
Don't share confidential details from past employers; interviewers notice discretion, and you can describe work without naming secrets.
